planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded-to-sunny patio container in bright indirect to full sun in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; cylindrical snake plant is extremely drought-tolerant and far more likely to be killed by overwatering than neglect.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded-to-sunny patio container in bright indirect to full sun in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; cylindrical snake plant is extremely drought-tolerant and far more likely to be killed by overwatering than neglect. Thick, rigid, cylindrical leaves rise straight up from the base like a cluster of gray-green spears banded with faint darker striping, a striking architectural silhouette very different from the flat-leaved snake plants more commonly grown, and the leaves are sometimes braided together for a novelty potted specimen. Native to dry, rocky regions of Angola and the Congo, it stores water in its succulent leaves and tolerates weeks of neglect, low light, and irregular watering, making it one of the toughest and most forgiving houseplants available. Water only when the soil is completely dry, provide as much bright light as possible for the fastest growth, and avoid cold drafts below the mid-50s Fahrenheit.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Moonshine snake plant holds its pale silvery color best out of direct hot sun, which can bleach or scorch the broad leaves.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Moonshine snake plant holds its pale silvery color best out of direct hot sun, which can bleach or scorch the broad leaves. Broad, solid, pale silvery-green leaves with a subtle darker green margin form an upright fan distinct from the horizontally banded, dark green leaves of the classic snake plant, giving this cultivar a cool, almost metallic glow that stands out in a low-light interior. Like other snake plants it stores water in thick, succulent leaves and tolerates long stretches of neglect and low light, making it one of the most forgiving houseplants for offices, hallways, and other spots that receive little natural light. Water only when the soil is fully dry, and divide congested clumps to propagate or refresh an overcrowded pot.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Bird's Nest snake plant's compact rosette habit makes it well suited to a small pot, dish garden, or tabletop planting.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright indirect light in fast-draining, sandy or cactus-type potting mix; Bird's Nest snake plant's compact rosette habit makes it well suited to a small pot, dish garden, or tabletop planting. Broad, dark green leaves banded with lighter gray-green markings spiral outward from a central point into a low, dense, bird's-nest-like rosette rarely more than a foot across, a dwarf, clumping sport of the classic upright snake plant discovered in the 1940s. Its diminutive size and slow growth make it an easy, long-lived houseplant for a windowsill, desk, or terrarium-style dish garden, tolerating the same range of low light and infrequent watering that makes larger snake plants so forgiving. Water only when the soil is fully dry and avoid overpotting, which encourages root rot in this slow-growing succulent.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Raven ZZ plant tolerates the same low light and infrequent watering as the standard green ZZ plant and is equally forgiving of neglect.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Raven ZZ plant tolerates the same low light and infrequent watering as the standard green ZZ plant and is equally forgiving of neglect. New leaflets emerge bright lime-green and darken over several weeks to a deep, glossy near-black, giving mature plants a dramatic, almost otherworldly color unlike any other common houseplant, while retaining the same thick, water-storing rhizomes and waxy, pinnate leaves as the species. It tolerates low light, infrequent watering, and general neglect better than almost any other foliage houseplant, making it a favorite for offices and low-light interiors, but grows fastest and darkest with bright indirect light. Allow the potting mix to dry out well between waterings, since the plant's rhizomes rot quickly in constantly wet soil.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; raindrop peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and stems and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; raindrop peperomia stores water in its thick leaves and stems and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings. Thick, glossy, deep green leaves are shaped like plump, upside-down teardrops or raindrops, growing on upright, fleshy stems in a naturally neat, bushy rosette that needs little pruning or shaping to look tidy. Native to South American forests, it is a semi-succulent species that tolerates missed waterings far better than soggy soil, making it a low-maintenance choice for a bright bathroom, kitchen windowsill, or office desk. Let the top half of the potting mix dry before watering again, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings rooted in water or moist soil.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Furry Feather calathea wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained potting mix; Furry Feather calathea wants high humidity and consistent moisture and is frost-tender outside zones 10-11. Long, narrow, wavy-edged leaves are covered on both surfaces with a soft, velvety fuzz, deep green on top and rich burgundy-red beneath, a plush, tactile texture unlike the smoother, glossier leaves of most other calatheas. Native to the humid forest floor of Brazil, it shares the family's characteristic nyctinastic movement, folding its leaves upward at night and lowering them again by day, and it thrives in the higher humidity of a bathroom, kitchen, or grouped plant display. Provide a humidifier or regular misting to prevent the notoriously crispy leaf edges calatheas develop in dry indoor air, and use distilled or rain water if tap water causes browning.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Drunkard's Dream is an epiphytic forest cactus and needs the same airy, orchid-bark-based mix and irregular watering as other jungle cacti.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in bright, indirect light in loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; Drunkard's Dream is an epiphytic forest cactus and needs the same airy, orchid-bark-based mix and irregular watering as other jungle cacti. Slender, jointed, bottle- or club-shaped stem segments branch repeatedly into an oddly whimsical, top-heavy tangle that gives the plant its playful common name, with small, bright yellow-orange, bell-shaped flowers appearing at the stem tips in late winter and spring. Native to the humid Brazilian rainforest canopy, where it grows perched on tree branches rather than rooted in soil, it prefers bright, filtered light rather than the intense direct sun of desert cacti and appreciates higher humidity than most succulents. Its arching, branching stems make it a natural fit for a hanging basket, and it is propagated easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before potting.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
